product_from_film: Friend is a wearable pendant companion that sends named, context-related messages to a phone.
explains_well: The same pendant-to-phone message pattern appears during a walk, gaming and a meal, making companionship concrete.
unclear: The film does not explain when the pendant listens, when a touch is needed, or how a conversation becomes a phone reply.
scenario: Carry a named companion through everyday moments and receive short comments on a phone.
product_clear_basis: The garden sequence links the worn pendant and a named phone notification; the gaming and meal scenes clarify the repeated companion pattern.

categories.finding: Garden companion → gaming tease → meal comments → rooftop intimacy → preorder.
The garden opens with a human outing and an unexplained brand, delaying the object’s role.
The first phone response suggests companionship around 23s; later scenes repeat and strengthen that reading.
Wide scenes alternate with pendant and phone inserts; the rooftop view becomes closer across sampled states. Exact cuts and camera movement unverified.
The repeated pendant, named message and reaction link otherwise separate settings.
Sunlit greenery, dim gaming light and a brick work room distinguish everyday contexts.
Names and brief messages give the companion a personality; the close gives a clear price and URL.
ASR supports casual scene dialogue but does not establish heard performance or the companion’s audio behavior.
Music character and structure are unverified.
Effects and their sources are unverified.

categories.finding: Pendant and notification inserts convey the premise without dialogue; the longer rooftop exchange needs dialogue context.
Object close-ups interrupt wider social scenes at the points where the companion becomes relevant.
Three brief use cases lead to a roughly thirty-second rooftop scene, shifting from function toward relationship.
Short context-related replies are the shown benefit; setup, sensing and response controls remain absent.
The replies and human reactions frame the device as company and playful attention; actual audience response is unmeasured.
Touch or wearing the pendant precedes messages, but the film does not establish a consistent trigger rule.
Ambient awareness, actual response generation, privacy, availability and price are not independently verified; visible scenes are demonstrations of a premise.
Using named messages across varied everyday situations gives an abstract companion idea a repeatable visual form.
Make the interaction rule visible once.
